title: Enabling Private High-Performance Production AI Inference with NVIDIA Confidential Computing | NVIDIA Technical Blog
gist: NVIDIA benchmarked confidential-computing (CC) inference on 8x B200 GPUs running DeepSeek-R1 via TensorRT LLM, showing CC-aware framework adaptations keep throughput loss under 4% and latency overhead under 5% versus CC-off -- positioning NVIDIA's hardware+software co-design (Blackwell CC plus TensorRT LLM) as the differentiator for running sensitive/regulated AI inference in production without a heavy performance tax.

insights.claim: NVIDIA Confidential Computing provides a pathway for running LLM inference securely on trusted hardware using memory-encrypted confidential VMs, confidential GPUs, and encrypted NVLink, aimed at personal, enterprise, and regulated settings where inference processes sensitive information and proprietary model context.
insights.speaker: Lorna Aine
insights.so_what: Positions confidential computing as a prerequisite for regulated-industry and enterprise AI adoption (healthcare, finance, government); NVIDIA baking this into Blackwell silicon plus its own inference stack (TensorRT LLM) creates a compliance-driven demand channel that competitors without full-stack control (chip + secure VM + inference runtime) struggle to match.
insights.quote: NVIDIA Confidential Computing (CC) provides a pathway for running these workloads securely using memory-encrypted confidential virtual machines (CVMs), confidential GPUs, and encrypted NVIDIA NVLink.

insights.claim: Running inference frameworks in a CC-enabled environment changes core runtime assumptions behind memory movement, timing, scheduling, and multi-GPU communication, introducing performance overhead unless the runtime adapts -- meaning the inference framework and confidential computing environment must be optimized together.
insights.speaker: Lorna Aine
insights.so_what: This is the core moat argument: security-with-performance in AI inference is a systems co-design problem, not a checkbox feature, so vendors owning both the silicon/hypervisor and the inference runtime (NVIDIA + TensorRT LLM) can deliver materially better secure-inference economics than piecemeal or open alternatives.
insights.quote: Maintaining high performance therefore requires the inference framework and the confidential computing environment to be optimized together.

insights.claim: High request volume amortizes fixed encryption costs by overlapping stalls with other work, which masks CC overhead; to expose the true worst-case overhead, NVIDIA's methodology deliberately selects workloads with long input context, extended output generation, and low concurrency.
insights.speaker: Lorna Aine
insights.so_what: A reusable benchmarking framework: investors/engineers evaluating any vendor's 'confidential computing overhead' claims should check whether the test workload was chosen to expose (not hide) worst-case overhead -- NVIDIA's stated methodology here is unusually rigorous and self-critical, lending credibility to the reported numbers.
insights.quote: To expose these effects, select a workload with a long input context, extended output generation, and low concurrency.
insights.locator: Selecting a workload to expose CC overhead

insights.claim: The benchmark used the DeepSeek-R1-0528-NVFP4 model on TensorRT LLM (PyTorch backend) with 32K input/1K output tokens, concurrency levels of 1, 2, 4, 8, and 16, tensor parallelism TP=8, FP8 KV cache, on a single NVIDIA DGX B200 system (8 B200 GPUs) with Intel TDX as the confidential computing platform.
insights.speaker: Lorna Aine
insights.so_what: Confirms NVIDIA is running confidential-computing benchmarks on flagship open-weight reasoning models (DeepSeek-R1) at production-realistic long-context settings, signaling this is being validated for real enterprise workloads, not synthetic toy tests.

insights.claim: Across concurrency levels 1 through 16, enabling confidential computing (CC on) retained 96.1% to 98.2% of CC-off output-token throughput, while mean Time Per Output Token (TPOT) overhead stayed within 1.2% to 4.3% versus the CC-off baseline.
insights.speaker: Lorna Aine
insights.so_what: This is the headline economic number: confidential inference on NVIDIA's stack costs under ~4% throughput and under ~5% latency versus unencrypted inference, a small enough tax that regulated enterprises could adopt secure AI inference on NVIDIA hardware without materially higher unit economics -- a potential incremental demand driver for Blackwell GPUs in regulated verticals.
insights.quote: CC on retained 96.1– 98.2% of CC off output-token throughput, while mean TPOT remained within 1.2% to 4.3% of the baseline.

themes.theme: Engineering mitigations that preserve performance under CC

insights.claim: In B200 confidential computing, host-to-device data transfers must pass through a software-encrypted bounce buffer because the GPU cannot directly access protected CVM memory, which breaks pinned memory's usual asynchronous-transfer advantage and can block the calling thread on some copies.
insights.speaker: Lorna Aine
insights.so_what: Illustrates a specific, non-obvious hardware constraint of confidential GPU computing (no direct GPU access to encrypted host memory) that any framework must work around -- a technical detail that raises the bar for competitors trying to replicate NVIDIA's CC performance without similarly deep systems engineering.
insights.quote: In the B200 CC, host-to-device transfers pass through a software encrypted bounce buffer because the GPU cannot directly access protected CVM memory.

insights.claim: TensorRT LLM mitigates the host-to-device bottleneck via CC-aware memory selection (pageable memory instead of pinned memory for affected paths) and moves repeated token/sampling-data readback to an asynchronous worker so protected copies don't block the main scheduler during decode.
insights.speaker: Lorna Aine
insights.so_what: Concrete evidence that NVIDIA is shipping CC-specific code paths inside TensorRT LLM (tracked via public PRs #11573 etc.), reinforcing that the performance advantage is embedded in software IP, not just hardware -- a durable, hard-to-copy advantage since it requires framework-level changes maintained over time.

insights.claim: Under confidential computing, CUDA-event timestamps produced an unstable timing signal that could cause TensorRT LLM's kernel autotuner to select a slower tactic; the mitigation is to use the GPU's %globaltimer for tactic measurement under CC while retaining CUDA events outside CC.
insights.speaker: Lorna Aine
insights.so_what: Shows CC can silently degrade kernel-selection quality (not just add direct overhead) if unaddressed -- a subtle correctness/performance risk that naive CC deployments (without vendor-specific tuning) could hit without realizing it, reinforcing the value of using NVIDIA's own optimized stack.
insights.quote: In the tested CC configuration, CUDA-event timestamps produced an unstable timing signal, which could cause the autotuner to select a slower tactic.

insights.claim: NVLS (NVLink SHARP) multicast is not available in B200 confidential computing configurations, so NCCL_SYMMETRIC loses its intended multicast benefit and may still incur memory registration and cross-rank synchronization costs before falling back to a non-multicast collective path; frameworks targeting CC should detect NVLS availability and choose latency-minimizing communication algorithms accordingly.
insights.speaker: Lorna Aine
insights.so_what: Reveals a real feature trade-off in current-generation (B200) confidential computing -- loss of NVLink SHARP multicast under encryption -- that multi-GPU inference/training frameworks must explicitly work around; watch future GPU generations (e.g., Vera Rubin) for whether this constraint is lifted, which would further reduce CC's performance tax.
insights.quote: NVLS (NVLink SHARP) multicast is not available in B200 CC configurations.

insights.claim: NVIDIA's stated position is that confidential computing does not remove the need for performance engineering but makes framework awareness even more important, and that security configuration and inference optimization should be treated as a single, full-stack deployment problem rather than separate concerns.
insights.speaker: Lorna Aine
insights.so_what: This full-stack framing is effectively a sales argument for staying on NVIDIA's integrated hardware-plus-software stack rather than mixing best-of-breed components from different vendors, since only the integrated stack has been shown (in this benchmark) to hold overhead under 5%.
insights.quote: Confidential computing does not remove the need for performance engineering—it makes framework awareness even more important.
insights.locator: Get started with NVIDIA Confidential Computing
